questions.stem: A 27-year-old client newly diagnosed with HIV is reviewing what was taught about transmission before going home to live with a partner and a roommate. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I can share a kitchen and bathroom with my roommate."
"My partner should talk to a provider about taking PrEP."
"I can share my razor if I rinse it well after each use."
"I'll use condoms until my viral load is undetectable."

rationale.correct: HIV spreads through blood, sexual fluids, birth and breastfeeding; items that may carry blood, such as razors, are never shared.

perOption.a: HIV is not spread by sharing household facilities.
perOption.b: Pre-exposure prophylaxis protects an HIV-negative partner.
perOption.c: Razors and toothbrushes can carry blood, so they are never shared.
perOption.d: Condoms reduce sexual transmission while the virus is detectable.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with HIV has had an undetectable viral load for 8 months on daily antiretroviral therapy. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: "If I stay undetectable, I won't pass HIV to my partner through sex."
"Since I'm undetectable, I'm cured and can stop taking my medicine now."
"I don't need any more blood tests while my virus stays this low."
"Being undetectable means it's safe for me to share needles now."

rationale.correct: Daily ART keeps the virus suppressed; U=U applies to sexual transmission only.

perOption.a: Undetectable = untransmittable (U=U) for sexual transmission with sustained viral suppression.
perOption.b: Stopping ART lets the virus rebound.
perOption.d: U=U applies to sexual transmission; sharing needles is still unsafe.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach about viral suppression and transmission.

questions.stem: A client with HIV who stopped antiretroviral therapy 4 months ago has had a dry cough and shortness of breath for 3 days. The temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), heart rate 108/min, respirations 26/min and SpO2 89% on room air. The CD4 count is 140 cells/mm3, and the chest x-ray shows bilateral diffuse infiltrates. Which prescription should the nurse carry out first?

options.text: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula at 4 L/min
Give IV trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Collect an induced sputum specimen
Give prednisone 40 mg by mouth

rationale.correct: In suspected Pneumocystis pneumonia, support oxygenation first, then give TMP-SMX, with steroids when hypoxemia is significant.

perOption.a: Hypoxemia is the most immediate threat, so oxygen comes first.
perOption.b: This treats the likely Pneumocystis pneumonia, but oxygenation comes first.
perOption.c: The specimen helps confirm the diagnosis but does not treat the hypoxemia.
perOption.d: Steroids are used in moderate to severe PCP, but not before oxygen.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize care for a client with HIV and pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old client starting daily oral HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) asks what follow-up is needed. What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: "You'll have an HIV test now and about every 3 months on PrEP."
"Once you start, you won't need any more testing."
"PrEP also protects you against other sexually transmitted infections."
"You'll take it on the days you have sex."

rationale.correct: PrEP: daily or long-acting medication, with HIV and STI testing every 3 months and kidney monitoring.

perOption.a: Regular testing makes sure HIV is not being treated with PrEP alone and checks kidney function.
perOption.b: Regular testing is required.
perOption.c: PrEP prevents HIV but not other STIs.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: While recapping a needle used on a client with HIV, a nurse sticks a finger, and it bleeds. The nurse is wearing gloves. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Remove the glove and wash the site with soap and water
Squeeze the finger hard and soak it in bleach for a few minutes
Finish the shift, then report it to employee health tomorrow
Ask for an HIV test in 6 months to see whether it was passed on

rationale.correct: Needlestick: wash with soap and water, report right away, and start PEP as soon as possible (ideally within 2 hours, at most 72).

perOption.a: Immediate cleaning reduces exposure; then the nurse reports it and is evaluated for post-exposure prophylaxis.
perOption.b: Squeezing and caustic agents are not recommended.
perOption.c: PEP works best when started within hours.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with HIV is starting a once-daily antiretroviral regimen. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take my pills at the same time each day with my breakfast."
"I'll skip a dose now and then on days when I'm feeling well."
"I'll ask before taking any new medicines, herbs or supplements."
"I'll keep going to my appointments for viral load tests."

rationale.correct: ART adherence prevents resistance and keeps the virus suppressed.

perOption.a: Consistent timing keeps drug levels steady.
perOption.b: Missed doses let the virus become resistant.
perOption.c: Many drugs and supplements interact with ART.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with advanced HIV and a CD4 count of 90 cells/mm3 is going home. Which symptoms should the client report as possible opportunistic infections? Select all that apply.

options.text: A fever that does not go away
A cough lasting more than a week
White patches in the mouth
New blurred vision or floaters
A gradual weight gain
Better appetite than before

rationale.correct: Report fever, cough, thrush, vision changes, diarrhea, headache and weight loss.

perOption.a: Persistent fever may mean infection.
perOption.b: This may suggest TB or Pneumocystis pneumonia.
perOption.e: This is not a sign of infection.
perOption.f: This is not a sign of infection.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach warning signs of opportunistic infections.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old client with systemic lupus erythematosus has a butterfly rash and joint pain that flared after a beach vacation. Which instruction is most important?

options.text: "Use sunscreen and cover up, and avoid the midday sun."
"Spend a little more time in the sun to dry out the rash."
"Use a tanning bed instead of the sun to build a base tan."
"Stop your medicines until the flare settles down."

rationale.correct: SLE: avoid the sun, manage fatigue, prevent infection and monitor the kidneys.

perOption.a: Sunlight can trigger lupus flares.
perOption.b: Sun worsens lupus.
perOption.c: UV light from tanning beds also triggers flares.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old client with systemic lupus erythematosus has new swelling of the ankles, foamy urine and a blood pressure of 152/96 mm Hg. The creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 1.4 mg/dL in a month. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Lupus nephritis
Dehydration from a flare
Drug-induced liver injury
A urinary tract infection

rationale.correct: Lupus nephritis is a serious complication; monitor urine protein, creatinine and blood pressure.

perOption.a: Kidney involvement causes proteinuria, edema, hypertension and a rising creatinine.
perOption.b: Dehydration does not cause edema and foamy urine.
perOption.c: This does not fit these findings.
perOption.d: A UTI does not cause edema and heavy proteinuria.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with lupus has taken hydroxychloroquine for 4 years and asks what follow-up care is needed while on it. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Have regular eye exams to check the retina."
"Have a hearing test every month while taking it."
"You'll need a weekly INR blood test."
"No special follow-up is needed for this medicine."

rationale.correct: Hydroxychloroquine: baseline and yearly eye exams after the first few years.

perOption.a: Hydroxychloroquine can cause retinal toxicity, especially with long-term use.
perOption.b: Hearing is not the main concern.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old client with rheumatoid arthritis is starting methotrexate 15 mg once a week and folic acid daily. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take my folic acid daily, just the way the doctor told me to."
"I'll take a methotrexate tablet each day so it works faster."
"I'll stop drinking alcohol while I'm on this medicine."
"I'll keep using reliable birth control while I take it."

rationale.correct: Methotrexate for RA: once weekly, with folic acid, no alcohol, contraception and monitoring of the CBC and liver tests.

perOption.a: Folic acid reduces side effects.
perOption.b: Taking it daily by mistake has caused fatal toxicity; it is a weekly dose.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach safe use of weekly methotrexate.

questions.stem: A client with Crohn disease who emigrated from a country with high rates of tuberculosis is about to start adalimumab. Which test should the nurse make sure has been done first?

options.text: Screening for latent tuberculosis
A bone density scan
Pulmonary function testing
A baseline echocardiogram

rationale.correct: Before TNF inhibitors and other biologics: screen for TB and hepatitis B, and watch for infection.

perOption.a: TNF inhibitors can reactivate latent TB.
perOption.b: This is not required.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Screen before starting a TNF inhibitor.

questions.stem: A client takes tacrolimus twice a day after a kidney transplant 2 months ago and enjoys grapefruit with breakfast. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Avoid grapefruit, and keep your blood level appointments."
"You can stop the tacrolimus once your kidney function is normal."
"Ask for live vaccines to protect you from infections."
"Take the tacrolimus on the days when you have a fever."

rationale.correct: Calcineurin inhibitors: nephrotoxicity, infection risk, drug and food interactions, and lifelong adherence.

perOption.a: Grapefruit raises tacrolimus levels, which must be monitored.
perOption.b: Stopping causes rejection.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach about immunosuppressant therapy after transplant.

questions.stem: During the admission interview before surgery, a client lists several food allergies that cause an itchy mouth and lips. The client is scheduled for an abdominal hysterectomy, and the surgical team uses gloves and catheters. Which food allergy suggests the client may also be allergic to latex?

options.text: Avocado
Strawberry
Wheat
Egg

rationale.correct: Latex-fruit syndrome: avocado, banana, kiwi and chestnut; use latex-free equipment and tell the team.

perOption.a: Avocados, bananas, kiwi and chestnuts cross-react with latex.
perOption.b: Strawberries are not a common latex cross-reactor.
perOption.c: Wheat is not a latex cross-reactor.
perOption.d: Eggs are not a latex cross-reactor.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client whose record says "penicillin: anaphylaxis (throat swelling) in 2019" is prescribed IV cefazolin 30 minutes before surgery. The surgical team is waiting. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Contact the provider to confirm before giving it
Give it, because cefazolin is not a penicillin
Give half the dose and watch the client closely
Give diphenhydramine first, then give the cefazolin

rationale.correct: Always clarify an order that may conflict with a documented severe allergy, even under time pressure.

perOption.a: Cross-reactivity is low, but a history of anaphylaxis needs the provider's review.
perOption.b: This ignores a serious allergy history.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a possible antibiotic cross-allergy.

questions.stem: The nurse is starting the first dose of IV ceftriaxone for a client with pneumonia who has no known allergies. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stay close and watch for an allergic reaction early on
Start it and check back on the client in 2 hours
Push it quickly to get the antibiotic in faster
Run it through the line with the client's blood

rationale.correct: Monitor closely during the first 15 to 30 minutes of a first-dose infusion.

perOption.a: Anaphylaxis often happens early with a first dose.
perOption.b: Early monitoring is needed.
perOption.d: Drugs are not mixed with blood.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old client has been taking clindamycin for 7 days for a dental abscess and calls the clinic with several concerns. Which report should the nurse address first?

options.text: Six watery stools a day with cramps
Mild nausea after each dose
A metallic taste in the mouth
A mild headache in the evening

rationale.correct: Antibiotics, especially clindamycin, can lead to C. difficile; frequent watery diarrhea is reported promptly.

perOption.a: This suggests C. difficile infection.
perOption.b: This is less concerning.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old client who takes prednisone for COPD started ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection 3 days ago. The client calls reporting sudden pain and swelling at the back of the right heel. What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: "Rest the leg and call your provider today about the pain."
"Stretch the calf several times a day to loosen the tendon."
"Take an extra dose of the antibiotic to clear the infection."
"Heel pain is common with age and is nothing to worry about."

rationale.correct: Fluoroquinolones: tendon rupture, QT prolongation, photosensitivity and C. difficile.

perOption.a: Fluoroquinolones can cause tendinitis and rupture, especially in older adults and with steroids.
perOption.b: Stretching could cause rupture.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old client is prescribed doxycycline for Lyme disease and works outdoors as a landscaper. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Avoid dairy near doses, use sun protection and stay upright after."
"Take each dose with a glass of milk so that it protects your stomach."
"Lie down for 30 minutes after each dose to prevent dizziness."
"Spend time in the sun, because sunlight helps it work."

rationale.correct: Tetracyclines: no dairy or antacids near doses, photosensitivity, stay upright after dosing, and avoid in pregnancy and young children.

perOption.a: Calcium reduces absorption, doxycycline causes photosensitivity, and it can irritate the esophagus.
perOption.b: Calcium binds doxycycline and reduces absorption.
perOption.d: Doxycycline makes the skin burn easily.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed metronidazole for 7 days for bacterial vaginosis and mentions a wedding this weekend. Which instruction is most important?

options.text: "Avoid alcohol during treatment and for 3 days after."
"Take each dose with grapefruit juice in the morning."
"Stop the pills once the symptoms have gone away."
"Drink extra coffee to stay alert while on it."

rationale.correct: Metronidazole: no alcohol during and for 3 days after, a metallic taste, and complete the course.

perOption.a: Alcohol with metronidazole causes severe nausea, vomiting and flushing.
perOption.b: This is not the concern.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a urinary tract infection is prescribed sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim twice a day. The client usually drinks two cups of coffee and little else. Which instruction helps prevent crystals forming in the urine?

options.text: "Drink plenty of water each day while you take it."
"Limit your fluids so the medicine stays concentrated."
"Take each dose with an antacid to protect the kidneys."
"Take both doses together at bedtime to rest the bladder."

rationale.correct: Sulfonamides: plenty of fluids, sun protection, and report any rash, which may signal Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

perOption.a: Fluids keep the urine dilute and prevent crystalluria.
perOption.b: This increases crystal formation.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old client is admitted with localized herpes zoster on the left chest wall. The lesions are not yet crusted. Which staff member should the charge nurse avoid assigning to this client?

options.text: A pregnant nurse who is not immune to varicella
A nurse who had chickenpox as a child
A nurse who received two doses of varicella vaccine
A nurse who had shingles last year

rationale.correct: Shingles can spread varicella to non-immune people; cover the lesions. Disseminated zoster needs airborne and contact precautions.

perOption.a: A person who is not immune can catch varicella from contact with the lesions.
perOption.b: This nurse is immune.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assign staff safely for a client with shingles.

questions.stem: A week after hiking in Connecticut, a client has a red rash about 8 cm wide with central clearing on the thigh where a tick was removed, along with fatigue and a low fever. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Early Lyme disease
Allergic contact dermatitis
Cellulitis of the thigh
Herpes zoster on the leg

rationale.correct: Lyme disease: erythema migrans, then possible joint, nerve and heart involvement; treated with doxycycline.

perOption.a: Erythema migrans is the hallmark of early Lyme disease.
perOption.b: This does not follow a tick bite this way.
perOption.c: Cellulitis is usually warm and tender, without central clearing.
perOption.d: Shingles follows a nerve path with blisters.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing discharge teaching for four clients going home on different antimicrobials, including an older adult with a kidney infection and a landscaper with Lyme disease. Each client asks what problems to watch for while taking the drug at home. For each drug, choose the adverse effect the nurse should monitor for most closely.

rationale.correct: Match each antimicrobial to its signature adverse effect.

perOption.r1:c1: Aminoglycosides damage the ear and kidney.
perOption.r2:c4: Ciprofloxacin can cause photosensitivity, but tendon rupture is the hallmark risk.
perOption.r3:c3: Metronidazole causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
perOption.r3:c4: This is not the key concern.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify key adverse effects of antimicrobials.

questions.stem: A client with MRSA bacteremia receives IV vancomycin every 12 hours at 0900 and 2100. The provider asks for a trough level before the 2100 dose. When should the nurse draw the blood?

options.text: Within 30 minutes before the 2100 dose
Right after the 0900 infusion has finished
One hour after the 2100 dose has finished
At any convenient time during the day

rationale.correct: Trough: just before the next dose. Peak: after distribution, with timing that depends on the drug.

perOption.a: The trough is the lowest level, just before the next dose.
perOption.b: This measures a peak.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Time a trough drug level correctly.
